name: Sam Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, sure, go ahead. Fair warning, I ramble and I make bad jokes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing electronic engineering with a robotics stream, so a normal week is lectures, a soldering lab, and way too much time in the maker space on campus. I live at home with my mum Marisol, who works as a dispatcher for a taxi firm, and I take the train in. Three evenings and Saturday morning I work at FixIt Kiosk in the shopping centre, repairing phone screens and charging ports. I use an AI assistant most days to help with circuit problems and to write code for my robot arm project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, cool, more time to build things. I'd tell my mates on the course that hype cycles come and go, and the real money is in people who can fix and build stuff. At FixIt my boss Reza would just shrug and carry on replacing screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan continues, and I'm fine with that. The only thing in my head is money, since I've got maybe three weeks of expenses saved and the train fare keeps rising. And my mum's taxi firm has been cutting dispatcher hours since the app arrived, even before any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at FixIt, and I'd ask Reza if I can start doing the board-level repairs, not just screens, because they pay more. I'd finish the robot arm and put it online, hoping someone notices. I'd also put away ten a week, on top of paying my mum a bit for food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. Slight low-level worry about money, but that's just life when you're eighteen and skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum's hours were cut. How does that affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because her pay dropped around fifteen percent last year. She hasn't said much, but we stopped getting takeaway on Fridays. I give her what I can from the repair wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would board-level repairs change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about double the rate, and it teaches me real electronics. If the phone repair trade survives, I could do it full-time in the holidays. It's a practical skill, and I like practical.

say: I'd say good, more **time** to build things, because hype cycles come and go.
I'd tell mates the real money is in people who can **fix and build**.
think: My plan continues, but with three weeks of **savings** and rising train fares I feel it.
My mum's **dispatcher** hours were already cut after the taxi app arrived.
do: Ask Reza to let me do **board-level repairs**, which pay about double.
Finish the robot arm and put it online.
Put aside ten a week and pay my mum for **food**.
feel: **Relaxed**, with a low worry about money.
S0.quote: The real money is in people who can fix and build stuff.
fieldNote: Sunny outlook rooted in **practical skill**, though his savings are only three weeks of expenses.
Family stress already visible: his mum's **hours** fell about fifteen percent and Friday takeaways stopped.
Wants to level up at the repair kiosk, a concrete income step.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday and evening shifts at FixIt Kiosk
Learn board-level repairs from Reza, which pay about double
Put ten a week into savings and pay my mum for food
Finish the robot arm and publish it online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where it gets interesting. Chatbots and coding assistants are already part of my day, and I'd say everyone on my course should be learning them properly. At FixIt I'd tell Reza to let me build a quick diagnostic helper for common faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the coding and checking part of my degree is the exposed bit, but the electronics and hardware side holds up longer. I'm in a lucky spot because robots spread slowly, so someone who can build a robot is useful. What bothers me is my mum. My mum's job as a dispatcher is exactly the sort of work the software takes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my project time into things that combine software and hardware, like sensors and motors. I'd use AI to speed up the boring bits so I can spend more time on the hard ones. And I'd help my mum learn the new dispatch tools the firm brings in, so she's the one who knows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit worried, in about equal parts. It's the family side that tips it into worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your mum's hours are cut again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take another shift at FixIt, and I'd give her more of the wages. We'd cut the TV subscription and the extras first. I'm not proud about it, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help her with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit with her on Sunday and run through the new dispatch screen. She learns by watching, not reading. I'd make a short video of the steps on my phone so she can replay it.

say: I'd say this is where it gets **interesting** and everyone on my course should learn AI properly.
I'd offer Reza a quick **diagnostic helper** for common faults.
think: The coding side of my degree is **exposed**, but electronics and hardware hold up longer.
My mum's **dispatcher** job is the sort the software takes first.
do: Focus projects on **sensors and motors**, where software meets hardware.
Use AI for boring bits and save my time for hard problems.
Help my mum learn the new **dispatch tools**.
feel: **Excited** and worried in equal parts, with family tipping it to worried.
S1.quote: My mum's job as a dispatcher is exactly the sort of work the software takes first.
fieldNote: Optimistic about his own path since **hardware** moves slowly, but his **mother's** job is the shadow over it.
Practical help: short phone videos of dispatch steps for his mum.
Willing to cut extras and give her more wages.

steps.text: Use AI to write boilerplate code for my robot arm
Take the sensors and motor control electives next term
Film short videos showing my mum the new dispatch screens
Offer Reza a diagnostic helper tool for common phone faults

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the wildest thing I've ever heard, and I'd be excited and terrified in one breath. I'd post about it, but mostly I'd talk to friends who'd get it. At FixIt I'd tell Reza that repair might last because robots take until 2031 to do hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my mum's job is gone within the two years, since dispatching is thinking work. She's the main earner and I'm a first-year with a loan. I'd be terrified, and I'm the sort of person who normally isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the course but treat it as a build-things programme, not a theory programme. I'd work every extra repair shift and learn board-level repair quickly, since hands-on work lasts a bit longer. I'd also look for a way to turn the robot arm into something people pay for, like a small automation kit for local workshops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because our household income depends on my mum. If I thought about it for too long I'd get a pit in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, I think the job might go, and I want us to plan together. I'd offer to cover the food and the phone, and I'd ask what her savings look like. She'd say I'm exaggerating, and I'd say please just listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the degree in this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it, but only if a paid apprenticeship came up that was clearly better. The degree is still a route to people and equipment. I'd stay unless somebody put money in front of me.

say: I'd say it's the **wildest** thing I've ever heard, exciting and terrifying together.
I'd tell Reza repair may last because hands-on robots take until **2031**.
think: My mum's job is likely **gone** within two years, and she's the main earner.
I'm a first-year with a **loan**, and I'm terrified.
do: Treat the course as a **build-things** programme, not a theory one.
Work every extra repair shift and learn board repair fast.
Turn the robot arm into a **kit** for local workshops.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a pit in my stomach because our income rests on my mum.
S2.quote: I'd say, Mum, I think the job might go, and I want us to plan together.
fieldNote: Normally cheerful, but in this scenario **household income** is the trigger for alarm.
Turns the conversation into planning with his **mother** and offers to cover food and phone.
Would only leave the degree for a clearly better paid apprenticeship.

steps.text: Sit down with my mum and go through her savings
Turn the robot arm into a small automation kit to sell
Learn board-level repairs from Reza as fast as possible
Work every extra shift at FixIt and bank the wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway. I'd tell people on the course to pick a niche and get good at it fast. At home I'd say to my mum that we should start building a cushion now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd graduate in 2029 into a world where the thinking work is nearly all done by machines, but robots for hands-on work are still two years out. That's a small window where people who can build and maintain robots could be in demand. I'd like to be in that window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a placement in a robotics firm, and I'd keep building my own projects. I'd keep working at FixIt so I'm not just a student, I'm someone with a trade. And I'd help my mum retrain, maybe into logistics planning or customer support for a hardware company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, but there's a chunk of worry about my mum. If she's out of work in 2031, we'd have to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your mum retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for a short course in logistics or supply chain, something with a certificate she can finish in six months. I'd research it, because she hates computers, and I'd sit with her while she signs up. I wouldn't push, but I'd make it easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you're wrong about the window for robot builders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've got a degree and a repair trade, both of which have value. I'd still be better off than somebody with only a degree or only a trade.

say: I'd say five years is a decent **runway**, so pick a niche and get good fast.
I'd tell my mum we should start a **cushion** now.
think: I'd graduate when robots for hands-on work are still two years out, a **window** for robot builders.
If my mum is out of work in 2031, we'd have to move **fast**.
do: Get a **placement** at a robotics firm and keep building my own projects.
Keep working at FixIt so I have a trade.
Help my mum find a short logistics course.
feel: **Energised**, with a chunk of worry about my mum.
S3.quote: I'd still be better off than somebody with only a degree or only a trade.
fieldNote: He sees a **window** for people who build and maintain robots and wants to be in it.
Keeps the repair job so he has a **trade** as well as a degree.
Plans to ease his mother into retraining without pushing.

steps.text: Apply for a robotics placement during second year
Study robot maintenance alongside my electronics modules
Find a six-month logistics course for my mum and sign her up
Keep the FixIt shifts and my repair trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do almost anything, so people should pick a direction and go. I'd be quite upbeat about it and I'd encourage friends to build things. At FixIt I'd tell Reza that his business will probably change but not vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get a degree, a decent first job, and a few years in robotics before the big change lands. My mum would be sixty by then, close to retirement, so her risk is smaller. I'd still help her prepare, but it wouldn't be a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a placement and start a small business building automation kits in my last year. I'd use AI to speed up the code and the paperwork. And I'd save regularly, starting with a small amount each week and growing it when I'm earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd still check my savings, but I'd feel like I'm on a decent road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a business in your last year. What would it sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small kits that let a workshop automate one boring job, like a sorting arm or a label printer. I'd start with the ones I've built for FixIt. If the first three customers like it, I'd carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop that from working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big firms selling cheaper kits, or the AI making the kit design too easy to copy. I'd keep it local and personal. People pay for a person who turns up, and that's how a repair shop works.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do almost anything, so pick a **direction** and go.
I'd tell Reza his business will **change** but not vanish.
think: I'd get a degree, a decent first job and a few **robotics** years before the big change.
My mum would be near retirement, so her **risk** is smaller.
do: Finish the degree with a **placement** and start an automation kit business in my last year.
Use AI to speed up code and paperwork.
Save a little each week and grow it as I earn.
feel: **Calm**, mostly; I'd feel like I'm on a decent road.
S4.quote: People pay for a person who turns up, and that's how a repair shop works.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him dream bigger: a small **kit business** built on repair-shop trust.
Notes the weak points: big firms and **easily copied** designs.
Less worried about his mum because she is near retirement.

steps.text: Sell small automation kits to local workshops in my last year
Use AI tools to write the code and paperwork for the kits
Save a fixed amount every week and raise it when I earn
Do a placement year at a robotics firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no contest. Mum's job would be gone and I'd have almost no time to get skills that matter. What would help is retraining that pays people while they study, small grants for starting a workshop business, and honest warnings from employers before they cut jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that a lot of people my age are told to be positive about all this. I try to be, but being positive is easier when your mum isn't the one in the firing line.

headlineQuote: Being positive is easier when your mum isn't the one in the firing line.
portrait: **Sam** is an eighteen-year-old electronic engineering and robotics student who repairs phones part time and lives with his mum.
He uses **AI tools** daily, builds things, and sees change as a chance to sell practical skills.
His cheerful surface covers a real worry: his mum's **dispatcher** job is the kind software takes first.
The fast scenario turns him alarmed because the household earner is exposed; ten years brings calm and a business plan.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because his mum's job would be gone and he'd have almost no time to build skills.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining that **pays** people while they study, small grants for workshop businesses, and honest early warnings from employers.
